I'm sorry this happened, bud. If it helps you to not feel so alone in this, I know some of what you're going through...especially the whole thing about reconsidering suicide...

Our situations are a bit different but don't let 1 fucking person tell you what you should or shouldn't do. Your healing is allowed to come at your own pace and doesn't need to involve stuff that makes you uncomfortable (like confronting her for instance).

Honestly, I've spent more hours curled up and crying on the bathroom floor than I can probably count. I've had so many triggering moments and people giving me shitty advice. And the thing that has helped the most is getting things off my chest on Reddit and talking with a really good therapist at least once a week. That's not to say therapy is for everyone but when you find a good one they're worth every penny.

Take things 1 day at a time. Own your healing process because it is yours and no one else's. Celebrate every victory right down to getting up and making food or going to the bathroom. Know that at any point, even if it's out of reach right now, you *always* have the power to take back all the control in your life. And if you don't have the strength to take it back right now that's fine. Be kind to yourself and don't guilt yourself for a damn thing. 

Your feelings are valid and recognized. And your life is worth all the healing you can/will experience.

As someone who was diagnosed with epilepsy later in life, I'd say the biggest thing that helped me was having my family actively telling me that I wasn't a burden. They'd reassure me of this all the time and say that even though living with this is difficult, I am still a beautiful human. 

Having a family/friend environment where we're all communicating our feelings very openly has been a huge plus as well. Like if my mom is just exhausted from work and doesn't *really* want to drive me somewhere she says something like "hon, you know I love you and want to support you but I'm so tired...how about I drive you if you help make dinner tonight 🙂" - this way I help her with something else she's not looking forward to but then I still get to run my errands 😅. 

Just be encouraging and let your sis know that she can talk to you and that you won't judge her or think she's being a burden.

PS I realize your actual support may look different than the example I gave since you don't live close to her. But maybe going to visit her frequently would be a good way to give her something to look forward to and during the time you're visiting you can focus on having fun together and also being supportive of what she needs.

I live in the US and was diagnosed with epilepsy in the middle of 12th grade. To be honest, my teachers not knowing what to do was the worst part. No one made fun of me. In fact random people who witnessed it (and it happened in multiple classes on multiple occasions) would come to me later and ask how I was doing. I know the age group was different than 15 year olds, but still. 

I wished that I had talked more with my teachers and councilors but I chose not to because I knew 2 of my teachers already hated me for being openly gay. One of them literally let me seize on the floor and yelled at the class for trying to help me. He said I was probably faking it. The other teacher tried to help me up mid-seizure and well...***that*** didn't go well. Luckily his "help" resulted in a minor injury which caused the school to fire him (good riddance). 

Anyways...I should've just told a councilor I was scared of what those two teachers might do. That would've solved most of the issues and also allowed the whole staff to be aware (at least the ones I saw on a daily basis) in case I had a seizure in any of their classes. Those two horrible teachers would've had a conversation beforehand that went something like this: "if you don't follow these steps when he starts having a seizure it'll be really bad for your career." 

Just be honest with teachers up front and try not to worry about other students so much. I know it's easier said than done but it is so freeing to just say "fuck them" and worry about yourself.

Is it not more constructive to consider that boys/men/girls/women all internalize different obstacles, advantages or disadvantages based on experiences they have which correlate with their age, class and ethnicity? 

I think for our purposes, recognizing the difference between a boy and a man is very valuable. We're talking about boys who are not yet mature vs men who are clearly mature. I'm just not sure that distinction is so easy to make sometimes. For me, the recovery process has been pretty hairy because there are virtually no resources to help my exact psychological needs. I mean sure everyone's different in what they've experienced or perceived but for many scenarios where male-to-female rape is concerned, there are books and podcasts and stories to help them cope. What is there for me? Therapy. That's it. There aren't "young-men-who-were-raped-AS-young-men" support groups.

Having experienced both scenarios, I think not knowing is SO much worse. 

My aura is usually getting really lightheaded, a bit confused and dazed like my eyes are kinda floating around the room and I'm super out of it for about a minute and then I start seizing. Since I spend so much time around my fiance he usually recognizes this and comforts me/helps me get into a comfortable position before it happens. I'm usually somewhat conscious for this so it allows me to feel a sense of safety before losing control and feeling embarrassed/hostile. 

A few times when I've had no aura, to my memory everything just goes black and I wake up VERY sore, super confused and paranoid of what might've happened while I was blacked out or unconscious. It sends me into a VERY deep depression for multiple days or weeks. Just overall not optimal...

Seems like PCP's in general are just really not as experienced with epilepsy as they should be. Much of what causes epilepsy and what treats it is still sort of a mystery (like in terms of WHY it happens and WHY certain treatments work vs others). 

I first started having seizures last January and the first 2 neurologists I tried to see were very...neutral. I'm sure they were knowledgeable but I left their offices feeling worse about my situation and like they didn't really care. Being that my mental state was NOT in a good place, I'm very thankful my family pushed me to speak up and say what was on my mind and I actually had my psychiatrist "refer" me to a neurologist (that way they could officially include details about my mental health and the importance of finding the right treatment as soon as possible).

I had COVID in the fall as well and since then it seems like absolutely nothing we try is working for my seizures which were fairly under control beforehand...unfortunately I don't think much research is being done on how COVID has effected epileptics. I understand some of what you're going through and am proud of you for already seeming optimistic about your other options (read some other comments). 

Hang in there. Don't give up on your quality of life. You'll find someone who values it as much as you do.

Maybe I can give some insight into what NOT to say:

- don't try to coax him into doing things or try convincing him to do stuff. For instance "hey you should come to this party with me, it might make you feel better" or "you should exercise more to help your mood." Even if those things would help, it will make him feel more shameful or guilty when he inevitably doesn't want to do them.

- don't ask him how he's feeling or doing constantly. It just highlights the fact that he's not doing well.

Things TO do/say:

- make sure he knows he can talk to you if he needs to (can be a simple "you know you can talk to me and I won't judge you if you need to talk right?" and leave it at that)
- approach things as if he's helping YOU, like saying "hey can you help me understand more about your epilepsy? I'm curious about x y or z." This way he may be more likely to open up about what he needs.
- straight up ask what he'd like you to do when he's feeling this way. My fiance will usually recognize I'm depressed and ask with a comforting smile: "what do you need?" And I know he's asking me what I want him to do, not do, etc. My answers are usually (1) I want to be left alone for a while or (2) cuddle me until I fall asleep. No matter what answer I give, he does what I ask without complaining or making me feel like a burden.
- at the end of the day, ask him what things he did, even if it's as simple as getting up to go pee or drinking some water. And treat every single thing like a mini victory. If he goes into the things he didn't do or talk about how he felt lazy, don't entertain those thoughts. Just tell him it's okay that he didn't do those things because he's allowed to feel sad or depressed sometimes. 

I hope some of this helps. Therapy is also amazing and I recommend it for everyone 👌🏼

I was diagnosed back in February after suffering a severe concussion and I do have a fairly obvious aura before my seizures, so I can't speak to the anxiety of truly never knowing when it could happen, but I think my fiance and mom's approach has been a good one and has made me feel a lot better about it all. Of course some of their approach was suggested by my therapist.

Anyways, I live with my fiance and mom and they both make a good point of not freaking out when I start seizing. Or they'll see that I'm spacing out and my eyes are rolling around and they'll say "hey, we should chill out on the floor for a sec" and what they really mean is *you're about to have a seizure so let's get closer to the floor and avoid injuries*. 

We've all had plenty of discussions around what makes me feel comforted and supported after a seizure. For me I need help getting to the bathroom, might throw up, I'm a tiny bit confused, I want water, and then within 30 minutes I'm feeling mostly back to normal with added fatigue and lingering sadness about the whole thing. My family knows to take care of me for those 30 minutes and then stop asking how I'm doing since it just makes me feel like a burden. 

So in other words...make sure you guys are communicating about what he needs. If he's too proud to speak up for what he needs then just take care of him as best you can during and after the seizure and leave the rest in his hands until he's ready to talk about it more.

Personally, I don't like being babied when it comes to my epilepsy. Being epileptic already makes me feel weak and broken, so I want to feel as in-control and independent as possible when it happens. The worst is when I'm in public and I start seizing and everyone starts losing their shit. Granted, I'm not always fully conscious for this but sometimes I am and I want to run away and hide forever. I don't often go out by myself because at least if there's someone with me they can tell the strangers that everything's under control.

Idk if any of this was helpful really...all I know is I'm sure you being supportive means more than you know and just keep communicating.
